promptHead: Athlete goal: 5K (Corrowmore Harvest 5K) on Sun Nov 15 2026, 10 weeks out, target run the whole way.

new.headline: A strong first week: three walk-runs, no pain and a steady heart rate. Next week stays at three days and makes the jogs a little longer, at 90 seconds each, run slower so they feel easy.

flags.title: How hard the jogs feel
flags.detail: Last week's jogs felt 6 to 7/10. Slow down until you can talk in full sentences, about 4 to 5/10, even if that means 8:30/km.

flags.title: Calf tightness
flags.detail: Tight the day after a run and gone by the next morning is normal for now. If it lasts into a second day or turns into pain, go back to 60-second jogs.

flags.title: Three run days, not more
flags.detail: Keep a non-running day between walk-runs. The dog walks on the other days are all the extra you need.

flags.title: Saturday as the check
flags.detail: If the 90-second jogs feel 5/10 or easier on Saturday and your calves are fine by Monday, the jogs get longer the week after.

answers.question: I want to be ready for the 5K in November. Should I run every day next week to get there faster?
answers.answer:
No. Stick to three runs a week, with a rest day or a dog walk between them. Your heart and lungs adapt quickly, but your calves, tendons and bones take longer, and they rebuild on the days off.

Your calves are already showing this. They are tight the day after each run and fine by the next morning. Running every day would pile new load on before the last lot has cleared, and an injury is the biggest threat to Nov 15.

You get there by making each jog a bit longer every week, not by adding days. On race day you need about 40 minutes of slow, steady jogging. Here is a rough path, which I will adjust each week:

| When | What the jogs look like |
| --- | --- |
| Aug 31 – Sep 6 | 90-second jogs between walks |
| Sep 7 – 20 | 2- to 5-minute jogs |
| Sep 21 – Oct 4 | 8- to 15-minute jogs |
| Oct 5 – 25 | 20 to 30 minutes without stopping |
| Oct 26 – Nov 8 | 35 to 40 minutes without stopping |
| Nov 9 – 15 | Lighter week, then race day |

If your legs handle these steps well, we can talk about a short fourth session later. Not yet.

new.analysis:
Your first week was exactly what a first week should be. You finished all three sessions with pain at 0/10 each time. Your heart rate barely moved from start to finish, which shows the effort was under control.

Your pacing was very even. The jogs came in around 7:40/km every time and the walks near 11:30/km. That consistency makes it easy to see what to change.

The one thing to change is how hard the jogs feel. Effort 6 to 7/10 is more than you need for short jogs, and about a quarter of your time was in zone 3, all of it from the jogs. Slower jogs will make the 90-second pieces manageable and go easier on your calves.

This week's step is longer jogs, not more days or faster running. Going from 1-minute to 90-second jogs is a small step that keeps you on track. The brisk walk at the start adds time on your feet without adding strain.

Your training calendar calls this a build phase, but for you that means building running time. Your goal is to run the whole way, and the hard part is how long each jog lasts. Speed sessions would add risk and do nothing for that goal.

The strength session uses squats, bridges and a plank, and leaves out calf work for now. Your calves are already doing plenty while they adapt. Stronger hips and thighs will help once the jogs get longer.

Each step only moves on when the last one felt comfortable. If a week feels too hard, we repeat it, and those repeat weeks are your lighter weeks. There is enough time before the race to allow for that.
